paragraphs: Achilles grieves for Patroclus—Thetis visits Hephaestus, and Hephaestus makes armor for Achilles.

So the fighting went on, blazing like a fire. Meanwhile Antilochus, the swift runner who had been sent as messenger, reached Achilles. He found him sitting by his tall ships, with a foreboding of what was in fact only too true. “Alas,” he said to himself in the heaviness of his heart, “why are the Achaeans scouring the plain again and crowding toward the ships? I pray the gods are not now bringing on me the sorrow my mother Thetis spoke of. She said that while I was still alive, the bravest of the Myrmidons would fall before the Trojans and no longer see the light of the sun. I fear the brave son of Menoetius has fallen through his own daring. Yet I told him to come back to the ships as soon as he had driven off the men who were bringing fire against them, and not to join battle with Hector.”

While he was turning this over in his mind, the son of Nestor came up and told him the sad news, weeping bitterly all the while. “Alas,” he cried, “son of noble Peleus, I bring you bad tidings. I wish they were untrue. Patroclus has fallen, and men are fighting around his naked body—for Hector holds his armor.”

A dark cloud of grief came over Achilles as he listened. He filled both hands with dust from the ground and poured it over his head. It spoiled his handsome face, and the grime settled on his fine new shirt. He threw himself down at full length, a huge man hugely stretched out, and tore his hair with his hands. The bondswomen whom Achilles and Patroclus had taken captive screamed aloud in grief. They beat their breasts, and their limbs gave way under them for sorrow. Antilochus bent over him, weeping and holding both his hands as he lay groaning, for he feared Achilles might cut his own throat with a knife. Then Achilles gave a loud cry. His mother heard it as she sat in the depths of the sea beside her old father, and she screamed. All the goddesses, daughters of Nereus, who lived at the bottom of the sea, came gathering around her. There were Glauce, Thalia and Cymodoce, Nesaia, Speo, Thoe and dark-eyed Halie, Cymothoe, Actaea and Limnorea, Melite, Iaera, Amphithoe and Agave, Doto and Proto, Pherusa and Dynamene, Dexamene, Amphinome and Callianeira, Doris, Panope, and the famous sea-nymph Galatea, Nemertes, Apseudes and Callianassa. There were also Clymene, Ianeira and Ianassa, Maera, Oreithuia and Amatheia of the lovely locks, with other Nereids who live in the depths of the sea. Their crowd filled the crystal cave, and they all beat their breasts while Thetis led them in their lament.

“Listen,” she cried, “sisters, daughters of Nereus, so that you may hear how heavy my sorrows are. Alas, woe is me, that I have borne the most glorious of sons. I bore him handsome and strong, a hero among heroes, and he shot up like a sapling. I tended him like a plant in a good garden and sent him with his ships to Ilium to fight the Trojans, but I shall never welcome him back to the house of Peleus. As long as he lives to look on the light of the sun, he is in heaviness, and though I go to him, I cannot help him. Still, I will go, to see my dear son and learn what sorrow has come to him, though he is still holding back from battle.”

She left the cave as she spoke, and the others followed her, weeping, and the waves opened a path before them. They came to the rich plain of Troy and rose up out of the sea in a long line onto the sand, at the place where the ships of the Myrmidons were drawn up in close order around the tents of Achilles. His mother went up to him as he lay groaning. She laid her hand on his head and spoke piteously. “My son,” she said, “why are you weeping like this? What sorrow has come to you now? Tell me; do not hide it from me. Surely Zeus has granted the prayer you made to him, when you lifted up your hands and begged that the Achaeans should all be penned in at their ships and bitterly regret that you were no longer with them.”

Achilles groaned and answered, “Mother, Olympian Zeus has indeed granted my prayer, but what good is that to me, now that my dear comrade Patroclus has fallen—the man I valued above all the others and loved as dearly as my own life? I have lost him. Hector killed him and then stripped off the wondrous armor, so glorious to see, that the gods gave to Peleus on the day they laid you in the bed of a mortal man. I wish you were still living among the immortal sea-nymphs, and that Peleus had taken some mortal woman as his bride. As it is, you will have endless grief for the death of a son you can never welcome home. No, I will not live or go about among mankind unless Hector falls by my spear and so pays me for killing Patroclus son of Menoetius.”
Thetis wept and answered, “Then, my son, your own end is near—for your death awaits you very soon after Hector’s.”

Then Achilles said in his great grief, “I would die here and now, since I could not save my comrade. He has fallen far from home, and in his hour of need my hand was not there to help him. What is left for me? I shall not return to my own land. I have been no rescue to Patroclus or to my other comrades, so many of whom have been slain by mighty Hector. I sit here by my ships, a useless burden on the earth—I, who in battle have no equal among the Achaeans, though in council there are better men than I. So let strife perish from among gods and men, and anger too, which can harden even a righteous man’s heart. It rises in a man’s soul like smoke, and the taste of it is sweeter than drops of honey. That is how Agamemnon has angered me. And yet—so be it, for it is over. I will force my soul into submission, as I must. I will go and hunt down Hector, who has killed the man I loved so dearly, and then I will meet my doom whenever Zeus and the other gods are pleased to send it. Even Heracles, the best beloved of Zeus—even he could not escape death, but fate and Hera’s fierce anger brought him down. I too will lie dead, if a like doom awaits me. Until then I will win fame. I will make Trojan and Dardanian women wring tears from their tender cheeks with both hands in the bitterness of their great sorrow. Then they will know that the man who has held back so long will hold back no longer. Do not hold me back, then, out of the love you bear me, for you will not move me.”

Then silver-footed Thetis answered, “My son, what you say is true. It is right to save your comrades from destruction. But your armor is in the hands of the Trojans. Hector carries it in triumph on his own shoulders. I know well that his boast will not last, for his end is close at hand. But do not go into the press of battle until you see me come back here. Tomorrow at break of day I will be here, and I will bring you good armor from King Hephaestus.”

With that she left her brave son. As she turned away she said to the sea-nymphs her sisters, “Dive down into the bosom of the sea and go to the house of the old sea-god, my father. Tell him everything. As for me, I will go to the cunning workman Hephaestus on high Olympus and ask him to give my son a suit of splendid armor.”
When she had said this, they dived at once beneath the waves, and silver-footed Thetis went on her way to bring the armor for her son.

So her feet carried the goddess to Olympus. Meanwhile the Achaeans were fleeing with loud cries before murderous Hector until they reached the ships and the Hellespont. They could not drag the body of Patroclus, the servant of Ares, out of range of the weapons showered on him. Hector son of Priam, with his host and horsemen, had caught up with it again, like the flame of a fiery furnace. Three times brave Hector seized the body by the feet, straining with might and main to drag it away and calling loudly to the Trojans. Three times the two Ajaxes, clothed in valor as in a garment, beat him off the body. But he was undaunted. Now he would charge into the thick of the fight, and now he would stand still and cry aloud, but he gave no ground. As upland shepherds cannot drive a famished lion away from a carcass, so the two Ajaxes could not scare Hector son of Priam away from the body of Patroclus.

And now Hector would even have dragged the body off and won imperishable glory, if Iris, swift as the wind, had not winged her way from Olympus as a messenger to the son of Peleus, telling him to arm. She came secretly, without the knowledge of Zeus and the other gods, for Hera sent her. When she had come close to him she said, “Up, son of Peleus, mightiest of all mankind. Rescue Patroclus, over whom this fearful fight is now raging by the ships. Men are killing one another, the Danaans defending the dead body, while the Trojans try to haul it away and take it to windy Ilium. Hector is the most furious of them all. He means to cut the head from the body and fix it on the stakes of the wall. Up, then, and wait here no longer. Shrink from the thought that Patroclus may become meat for the dogs of Troy. Shame on you, if his body suffers any kind of outrage.”
And Achilles said, “Iris, which of the gods sent you to me?”
Iris answered, “It was Hera, the royal wife of Zeus. But the son of Cronus does not know I have come, and neither does any other of the immortals who live on the snowy summits of Olympus.”

Then swift Achilles answered her, “How can I go up into the battle? They have my armor. My mother forbade me to arm until I should see her come, for she promised to bring me good armor from Hephaestus. I know of no man whose arms I could put on, except the shield of Ajax son of Telamon. And he surely must be fighting in the front rank, wielding his spear around the body of dead Patroclus.”

Iris said, “We know your armor has been taken. But go as you are. Go to the deep trench and show yourself to the Trojans, so that they will fear you and stop fighting. Then the exhausted sons of the Achaeans will gain a brief breathing space, which is hard to come by in battle.”

When Iris had spoken, she left him. Achilles, dear to Zeus, rose, and Athena threw her tasseled aegis around his strong shoulders. She crowned his head with a halo of golden cloud, and from it she kindled a glow of gleaming fire. As the smoke goes up into the sky from a city under siege on an island far out at sea—all day long the men sally out from the city and fight their hardest, and at the going down of the sun the line of beacon fires blazes up, flaring high for their neighbors to see, in case they may come with their ships and help them—so the light flared from the head of Achilles as he stood by the trench, going beyond the wall. But he did not join the Achaeans, for he heeded the charge his mother had laid on him.

There he stood and shouted aloud. Athena also raised her voice from far off and spread unspeakable terror among the Trojans. A trumpet rings out when the enemy is at the gates of a city and sounds the alarm. So rang the brazen voice of the son of Aeacus, and when the Trojans heard its clarion tones they were dismayed. The horses turned back with their chariots, sensing disaster, and the drivers were awestruck at the steady flame the gray-eyed goddess had kindled above the head of the great son of Peleus.

Three times Achilles raised his loud cry as he stood by the trench, and three times the Trojans and their brave allies were thrown into confusion. Twelve of their noblest champions fell beneath the wheels of their chariots and died on their own spears. To their great joy the Achaeans then drew Patroclus out of range of the weapons and laid him on a litter. His comrades stood mourning around him, and among them swift Achilles wept bitterly as he saw his true comrade lying dead on his bier. He had sent him out into battle with horses and chariots, and he was not to welcome his return.
Then Hera sent the busy sun, unwilling as he was, down into the waters of Oceanus. He set, and the Achaeans had rest from the tug and turmoil of war.

The Trojans, coming out of the fight, unyoked their horses and gathered in assembly before preparing their supper. They stayed on their feet, and no one dared sit down, for fear had fallen on them all because Achilles had shown himself after holding back from battle so long. Polydamas son of Panthous was the first to speak, a man of judgment, who alone among them could look both before and after. He was a comrade of Hector, and they had been born on the same night. With all sincerity and goodwill he spoke to them like this:—

“Think carefully, my friends. I urge you to go back to your city now and not wait here by the ships until morning, for we are far from our walls. As long as this man was at enmity with Agamemnon, the Achaeans were easier to deal with, and I gladly camped by the ships, hoping to take them. But now I am in great fear of the swift son of Peleus. He is so daring that he will never wait here on the plain, where Trojans and Achaeans fight with equal valor. He will try to storm our city and carry off our women. So do as I say, and let us retreat. This is what will happen. The darkness of night will hold the son of Peleus back for a while. But if he finds us here in the morning when he sallies out in full armor, we shall come to know him in good earnest. Glad will be the man who can escape and get back to Ilium, and many a Trojan will become meat for dogs and vultures—may I never live to hear it. If we do as I say, little as we may like it, we shall have strength in counsel during the night, and the great gates with the doors that close them will protect the city. At dawn we can arm and take our stand on the walls. He will regret it then if he sallies from the ships to fight us. He will go back when he has let his horses run their fill, driven in every direction under our walls, and he will have no mind to try to force his way into the city. Nor will he ever sack it. The dogs will devour him first.”

Hector looked fiercely at him and answered, “Polydamas, I do not like your words, telling us to go back and be penned inside the city. Have you not had enough of being cooped up behind walls? In the old days the city of Priam was famous all over the world for its wealth of gold and bronze. Now our treasures have been wasted out of our houses, and many goods have been sold away to Phrygia and lovely Meonia, because the hand of Zeus has lain heavily on us. But now the son of scheming Cronus has granted me to win glory here and to hem the Achaeans in at their ships. So stop your prating in this foolish, would-be wise way among the people. You will have no man with you. It shall not be. All of you, do as I now say—take your suppers in your companies throughout the host, keep your watches, and be wakeful, every man of you. If any Trojan is uneasy about his possessions, let him gather them and hand them out among the people. Better that these men have them than the Achaeans. At daybreak we will arm and fight around the ships. Granted that Achilles has come forward again to defend them, let it be as he wishes, but it will go hard with him. I shall not shun him. I will fight him, to fall or to conquer. The god of war deals out equal measure to all, and the slayer may yet be slain.”
